chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Sayf ibn 'Amirah, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man had wealth owed to him by another man, so the debtor denied it and took it away. Then afterwards, wealth came to be with the man whose wealth had been taken, from that same debtor. Can he take it from him in place of the wealth that man had taken from him? He (peace be upon him) said: Yes, but for this there is a statement (du'a) to be made: 'O Allah, I take this wealth in place of my wealth which He took from me, and I do not take what I take from it as treachery, nor as injustice.'

key_terms.جَحَدَهُ: denied it (refusing to acknowledge the debt)
key_terms.ذَهَبَ بِهِ: took it away / carried it off
key_terms.مَكَانَ: in place of / as compensation for

ai.seo_question: How does a creditor legally recover a denied debt by retaining the debtor's property?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi outlines the mechanism of debt offset (qabd), permitting a creditor to retain a debtor's funds to settle a previously denied debt, provided the creditor recites a specific supplication to ensure the act is not considered treachery (khiyanah) or injustice (zulm). Scholarly commentary emphasizes that this retention is a form of self-help remedy rather than a judicial seizure, with the supplication serving to purify the creditor's intent from arbitrary seizure. The ruling highlights the Shia legal principle of restoring equity when a debtor initially denies the obligation, balancing the creditor's right to recovery with the debtor's protection from unjust enrichment.
